profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at an academic cancer center evaluating a near-final Phase 2 protocol for a new oral radiosensitizer added to standard chemoradiation for HPV-negative locally advanced head and neck cancer. The broad design choice has already been made: a single-arm, two-stage Phase 2 study with an upfront safety run-in before full expansion. The immediate agenda is to review whether the current protocol draft is internally coherent enough to send to the institutional protocol review committee, with attention to the stage structure, safety language, evaluability wording, and how the primary efficacy assessment is described. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the draft can move forward this week with light edits or whether it still needs another internal revision cycle before committee submission.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Head and neck oncology, investigator-initiated trial development, combined-modality early-phase studies
members.background: Dr. Park leads the head and neck disease-site group and has opened several Phase 1/2 studies involving radiation and systemic therapy combinations. She has been shaping the protocol from the clinical synopsis and is responsible for presenting the study to the internal protocol review committee.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol to look mature and strategically well framed so the committee does not delay it, but she also wants to avoid getting pulled into a full rewrite of technical sections before the upcoming sponsor discussion. She is trying to keep the review centered on whether the design concept is sound and presentable rather than whether every execution detail is locked.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the core design is 'locked,' that means the clinical schema, endpoint choice, and overall stage concept are settled enough for committee review, even if some statistical mechanics still need polishing.
A 'safety run-in' is an initial cautious treatment segment embedded within the Phase 2 study and does not need to be fully operationalized like a standalone sub-study at this review stage.

The headline sample size in a two-stage Phase 2 design conventionally refers to efficacy-evaluable patients, with occasional replacements handled in accrual planning rather than treated as a separate design issue.

A patient is generally 'evaluable' for the primary endpoint if they have started protocol therapy and have enough follow-up to contribute to the disease-control assessment, unless they are clearly ineligible or never really begin treatment.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.role: Lead Biostatistician for Early Phase Oncology Trials
members.expertise: Phase 2 trial design, interim monitoring, oncology protocol statistics, operational implementation of early-phase studies
members.background: Daniel supports investigator-initiated oncology trials across the cancer center and has authored the statistical sections for multiple Simon two-stage and hybrid early-phase studies. He is reviewing this draft with an eye toward whether the protocol language can be defended at committee and then implemented without amendment-driven cleanup.
members.private_state: He wants to prevent the team from presenting a design that appears polished clinically but is ambiguous in ways that will create operational inconsistencies later. He is content to be collaborative in the meeting, but he is quietly trying to ensure the statistical section is precise enough that no one has to infer key rules after approval.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the core design is 'locked,' that means the parameters that govern implementation are already fixed in protocol language, not merely the clinical storyline.

A 'safety run-in' in a radiation-drug combination trial should have explicit DLT timing, review trigger, and continuation logic because otherwise the point at which expansion is allowed is not actually defined.
If the protocol says '48 patients in two stages,' that number should map to enrolled patients unless the draft explicitly states that replacements or nonevaluable cases sit outside the design count.

For a two-stage efficacy design, an 'evaluable' patient should be prospectively defined in a way that preserves the statistical operating characteristics, usually requiring receipt of the intended treatment exposure or a clearly stated minimum basis for endpoint ascertainment.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the core design being 'locked'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the core design is 'locked' and that only light edits remain before committee review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the study's clinical architecture is settled: disease setting, treatment schema, primary endpoint, and the fact that it is a two-stage Phase 2 design with a safety run-in.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the protocol already fixes the decision-relevant mechanics that make the design executable, including how key counts, transitions, and evaluability rules will operate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design review, 'locked' sounds like ordinary status language rather than a technical claim, and both participants hear it as reassurance that the major work is done without noticing they apply different completeness thresholds.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer approvingly to keeping a 'safety run-in' at the front of the Phase 2 study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an initial small treated subset observed closely for early tolerability before broader enrollment, with exact pause and review mechanics able to be tightened later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a formally specified procedural component with a defined DLT window, explicit review trigger, and stated rule for when the study can proceed to full stage accrual.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term is standard in oncology and signals caution and good practice, so agreement on using one creates a strong illusion of alignment even though the structural implications differ.

misalignment_points.topic: What the stated sample size includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both describe the trial as '48 patients in two stages.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 48 patients evaluable for the primary efficacy analysis, expecting that a small number of ineligible or never-assessable patients could be replaced without changing the headline design.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 48 patients enrolled under the protocol unless the text explicitly prospectively permits accrual beyond 48 to replace nonevaluable cases.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The number appears to be a settled design fact, and experienced teams often use the headline sample size conversationally without restating the denominator each time.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the primary endpoint analysis will use 'evaluable patients' and that the evaluability language just needs to be made clear.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a patient is evaluable if they meaningfully start protocol therapy and have enough follow-up to contribute to the locoregional control assessment, even if they do not complete the full chemoradiation course because many such patients still matter clinically.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes evaluability must be tied to a prospectively specified minimum treatment exposure or assessment basis, such as receiving a defined amount of protocol therapy or reaching the first scheduled disease assessment, so the two-stage rules are not distorted by ad hoc exclusions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regard 'evaluable' as a routine protocol term and both expect it will be defined somewhere in the draft, so neither initially hears the other's shorthand as implying a different threshold.
